headline: Test recovery with 20 easy minutes—or rest
summary: The snapshot is within 36 hours, but it predates last night, so today's sleep, sleeping heart rate and morning readiness are unavailable. Four days after the marathon, a short flat test jog is reasonable only if walking, stairs, energy and posterior-tibial symptoms are all normal; otherwise rest.

The marathon supplied 513 load points and remains the dominant stress.

recommendation.title: 20-minute flat recovery test jog, only if symptom-free
details: Before starting, require normal walking and stairs, no focal medial-ankle or arch pain, no altered gait, and no unusual fatigue or illness.
Run exactly 20 minutes on flat, predictable ground at conversational RPE 2–3; roughly 6:30–7:15/km is a ceiling guide, not a target.
Do not add strides, hills, tempo work, extra distance or loaded calf/foot strength today.
Judge the session by relaxed breathing and stable symptoms, not by forcing a generic heart-rate zone.
recommendation.alternative: Take complete rest, or walk gently for 20–30 minutes, if this morning feels worse than the latest available Garmin data or any pre-run gate is not met.
recommendation.reduce_or_stop: Stop immediately if posterior-tibial discomfort exceeds 2/10, rises as you run, becomes sharp or localised, or changes your stride. Do not run again if pain is worse later today or tomorrow morning; swelling, altered gait, illness or medical advice overrides Garmin scores.

signals.label: Time since marathon
signals.interpretation: A short movement test may be appropriate, but muscular and connective-tissue recovery is still incomplete even when device scores rebound.

signals.label: Recent concentrated load
signals.interpretation: The seven-day total includes a 42.74 km marathon plus a 6.99 km run the following day, favouring a minimal test rather than normal training.

signals.label: Missing morning recovery
signals.interpretation: It meets the 36-hour freshness rule but cannot confirm last night's sleep, sleeping HR, resting HR, Body Battery or today's readiness.

caveats: The snapshot window ends on 2 September and does not contain last night's sleep or today's recovery metrics.
The 14-night sleeping-heart-rate export contains no valid values, so sleeping HR cannot be compared with a recent range.
The latest available sleep record contains 65 bpm in its detailed average-heart-rate field while the dedicated overnight field is null.
Wrist heart-rate data from the 31 August run are internally inconsistent (145 bpm average and 190 bpm maximum), so they are not used to set today's intensity.
